clue.text: In which a churchwarden stands out

definitions.text: In which a churchwarden stands out

parts.words: In which a churchwarden stands out
parts.note: a churchwarden is also a long clay tobacco pipe, so this is a holder where such pipes are displayed upright

explanation.surface: A church official is conspicuous in some setting.
explanation.walkthrough: The churchwarden looks like a parish official, but here it is a long-stemmed clay pipe, and 'stands' is a literal stand for pipes.
explanation.definitionFit: A rack for pipes is a stand in which smoking pipes, a churchwarden among them, are stood and displayed.

clue.text: Attempt to store cooking vessel on top of larder

indicators.note: in a down clue the vessel sits above the attempt, coming first

parts.note: a pan is a cooking vessel
to try is to attempt

explanation.surface: Someone tries to put a saucepan up on the larder shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'on top of' means placed above, so the vessel comes first; 'to store' looks like a container signal but is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A larder is a small room or cupboard for keeping food, the same as a food store room.

clue.text: Temple of a deity old man's entering

indicators.note: the deity phrase goes into the father word, entering it

parts.note: old man is slang for father, so PA, with 's for is
a god is a deity

explanation.surface: An elderly man goes into a shrine of a god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is the usual slang for father; 'entering' signals the deity phrase going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiered tower used as a Buddhist or Hindu temple in East Asia.

clue.text: Exposition all there by end of June

parts.note: someone all there is sane and clear-headed, rational

indicators.note: the end of the month's name supplies its final letter

explanation.surface: An explanation is promised in full by late June.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of' takes E from June; 'by' is a link joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement setting out the reasons for something is an explanatory exposition.

clue.text: Support of knights for series of contests?

parts.note: medieval knights were champions, and to champion something is to support it, so the word is read as the state of being a champion

explanation.surface: Knights back a set of tournaments.
explanation.walkthrough: Knights jousted as champions; read playfully, the word means championing or support, while really it is a sports tournament series.
explanation.definitionFit: A competition decided over a series of games or rounds to find an overall winner.

clue.text: Shaded seat on a jumbo

parts.note: jumbo is a nickname for an elephant, not a jumbo jet, and the seat is the canopied carriage on its back

explanation.surface: A seat on a big plane is kept out of the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumbo' suggests an airliner; it is an elephant, and the shaded seat is the canopied carriage riders sit in.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the canopied seat strapped to an elephant's back in India, so a covered perch on an elephant.

clue.text: Finished first in the table, that's obvious

parts.note: over means finished

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the furniture word is taken

explanation.surface: A team boasts that coming top of the league was plain to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First in' takes T from table; 'the table' suggests a league, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done openly and plainly visible is evident, not hidden.

clue.text: Men in corps ordered under as strafe's beginning

indicators.note: the letters are put in a new order, rearranged
the first letter of the attack word is taken

explanation.surface: Soldiers are commanded to take cover as an air attack starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corps' suggests soldiers; it is the corps de ballet. 'Ordered' rearranges UNDER AS into DANSEUR, and 'beginning' adds S from strafe.
explanation.definitionFit: These are male ballet dancers, the men of a corps de ballet.

clue.text: Wren's construction in sacred setting, plainly

indicators.note: the sacred word forms the setting that holds the nest

parts.note: holy means sacred
a wren is a small bird and it builds a nest

explanation.surface: Christopher Wren's building in a holy place, simply described.
explanation.walkthrough: Wren looks like Sir Christopher, architect of St Paul's, but it is the small bird; 'setting' signals a container.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak frankly and truthfully is to speak plainly.

clue.text: Did it go to Falstaff's head when he hit the sack?

definitions.text: Did it go to Falstaff's head when he hit the sack?

parts.words: Did it go to Falstaff's head when he hit the sack?
parts.note: Falstaff, Shakespeare's drinker, loved sack (sherry); hitting the sack is going to bed, so this is a drink before sleep

explanation.surface: A question about whether Shakespeare's fat knight got drunk on sherry.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack is old sherry, Falstaff's favourite drink, and 'hit the sack' also means go to bed; a bedtime drink, or a cap worn on the head in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedtime drink is taken just before sleep, and the word also names a cap worn in bed, both suiting the head.

clue.text: Diminishing standard of writer with no new following

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument, so a writer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer without fresh readers has a declining level of quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diminishing standard' reads as falling quality, but it is a flag that tapers to a point; 'following' puts NO and N after PEN.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a long narrow flag tapering to a point, so a standard or banner that diminishes along its length.

clue.text: Recorded impressions of a criminal

parts.note: impressions here are marks pressed onto a surface by fingertips, taken and filed by the police, not a mimic's act

explanation.surface: An impressionist's recorded imitations of a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impressions' suggests impersonations; they are marks from a suspect's fingertips kept on police file.
explanation.definitionFit: Police take and keep the ridged marks left by a suspect's fingertips as identifying records.

clue.text: Exhibition in which 7 may perform

parts.note: the exhibition is a cowboy show, and it is also the title of a Copland ballet in which male ballet dancers (7-down) dance

explanation.surface: A display at which the answer to 7 might appear.
explanation.walkthrough: 7-down is DANSEURS, male ballet dancers; the cowboy show shares its name with Aaron Copland's ballet, so dancers can perform in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A show of cowboy skills such as bronco riding is a public exhibition, and Copland's ballet of that name is danced on stage.

clue.text: Be more polite, in a way? That's futile

definitions.text: Be more polite, in a way
definitions.meaning: pointing at people is rude, so doing it to a lesser degree is a more polite way to behave
futile means having no purpose or use

explanation.surface: Someone is told to mind their manners, and replies that it would be useless.
explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer is an instruction to point less, since pointing at people is thought rude.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without a point has no purpose, which is what futile means.

clue.text: Gilbert's modern model in brass

parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's Pirates of Penzance a character sings that he is the very model of a modern one, and brass means senior army officers

explanation.surface: W. S. Gilbert's up-to-date figure cast in metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like the metal of a statue; it is slang for high-ranking officers. Gilbert's patter song begins 'I am the very model of a modern...'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a senior army officer rank, one of the top brass, and the subject of Gilbert's famous patter song.

clue.text: Run more at random to get a number over the line

indicators.note: random here signals that the letters before it are shaken into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A cricketer runs more freely to get the score past a boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' is part of the fodder, so 'random' alone is the anagram signal; the answer is the top figure of a fraction.
explanation.definitionFit: In a fraction, the figure written above the dividing line is the top number.

clue.text: Deceitful couple, supplied with food, concealing bill

parts.note: a couple is two

indicators.note: the food word hides the bill inside itself

parts.note: fed means supplied with food
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: A pair eat well and hide the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' is an account, abbreviated in the usual way; 'concealing' signals a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypocritical person shows one face and hides another, so is deceitful.

clue.text: Crown left in ship's tender

indicators.note: the letter for left is placed inside the boat word

parts.note: a pinnace is a small boat carried by a ship as a tender

explanation.surface: A crown is left on board a ship's small boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' might be soft, but it is a boat serving a larger ship: a pinnace.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point or peak of something is its summit, its crowning point.

clue.text: Author's problem of no concern to dictator

definitions.text: Author's problem of no concern to dictator

parts.words: Author's problem of no concern to dictator
parts.note: a dictator here is someone who dictates to a secretary rather than holding a pen, so a hand ache from writing never troubles them

explanation.surface: A novelist's difficulty means nothing to a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' suggests a tyrant; it is someone who dictates words for others to write down, so never gets an aching hand.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a painful cramp of the hand from long spells of writing, a complaint of authors working by hand.

clue.text: Hollow warning of schoolboys to sailors

parts.note: cave (Latin 'beware') was British public-school slang called out when a teacher approached
RN is the Royal Navy, sailors

explanation.surface: Boys shout a warning to a group of sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: CAVE (pronounced KAY-vee) was British public-school slang to warn that a master was coming.
explanation.definitionFit: A large underground hollow or chamber in rock.

clue.text: Damage in attack

definitions.meaning: slang for the cost of something, as in 'what's the damage?'
to rush forward against an enemy

explanation.surface: Harm is done during an assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damage' is not harm but the price asked, as in 'what's the damage?'
explanation.definitionFit: A price is what one is billed, the 'damage'; and rushing at an enemy is an attack.

clue.text: Tycoon at home in more ornate surroundings

indicators.note: the more ornate word forms the surroundings, with the home word placed within it

parts.note: fancier means more elaborate or ornate
in means at home

explanation.surface: A rich businessman relaxes at home amid lavish decor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surroundings' is the container signal; the 'in' before 'more ornate' is only a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tycoon is a wealthy business magnate, and a person who manages large sums of money is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Common sense about new words relating to things

indicators.note: the sense word goes about, around, the new letter

parts.note: nous is British slang for common sense

explanation.surface: Common sense about modern vocabulary for objects.
explanation.walkthrough: NOUS (British for practical wit) goes 'about' N to give NOU-N-S.
explanation.definitionFit: The parts of speech that name people, places and objects.

clue.text: Land at this stretch of river

definitions.meaning: to land at a place is to arrive there
a straight length of river between bends

explanation.surface: Boats come ashore on a particular part of a river.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrive at a place is to get to it; and a straight section of river between two bends shares the same word.

clue.text: Something badly done has friend appearing for trial

parts.note: cock is old British slang for a mate or pal, as in 'wotcher, cock'
a defendant who is up is appearing before a court

explanation.surface: A botched job means a pal ends up in the dock.
explanation.walkthrough: COCK is old London slang for a mate; 'up before the magistrate' means facing trial.
explanation.definitionFit: A British colloquialism for a blunder or mess, a task that has been botched.

clue.text: King taking a winter break in Jersey or Guernsey, say

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase are broken up and put back together differently

explanation.surface: A monarch takes a winter holiday on one of the Channel Islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' scrambles A WINTER to NITWEAR after K. The islands are red herrings: a jersey and a guernsey are both woolly jumpers.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerseys and guernseys are knitted woollen sweaters named after the Channel Islands, examples of knitted garments.

clue.text: Taking care always to be in the right gear

definitions.text: Taking care always to be in the right gear

parts.words: Taking care always to be in the right gear
parts.note: gear here is clothing, not a car's gearbox: someone always careful to wear smart clothes

explanation.surface: A careful driver always makes sure to select the correct gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gear' sounds like driving, but it is clothes: a person always careful to look smart.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fond of smart, elegant clothes takes pains over what they wear.

clue.text: Set at odds and distance

definitions.meaning: to cause people to quarrel or become unfriendly
used as a verb, to keep someone at arm's length or cut them off

explanation.surface: Bets are placed on how far something travels.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate people is to set them at odds and put emotional distance between them.
